transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-14 16:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Marco Santos (Redwood SRE); Samira Patel, Liam O'Connor, Nina Gomez, Ethan Wu (AtlasHealth)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive on integrating Redwood's runtime observability with AtlasHealth's OpenTelemetry stack. Focus areas: token-level metrics, span design, KV cache / batching visibility, quantization impact on latency, and secure OTLP export for VPC/on-prem deployments.

Topics covered: OpenTelemetry spans for generation, token-level vs request-level metrics, sampling strategies, metric cardinality, dashboards (Grafana/Tempo/Jaeger), OTLP over TLS in VPC, sidecar vs daemonset, and cost/latency trade-offs.

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): alright hi everyone thanks for joining, we'll do a deep dive today on observability and tracing integration, um mostly around OpenTelemetry and token-level metrics for the runtime. quick intros please?
[00:12] Samira (AtlasHealth): hey thanks, Samira here, Head of ML, we're evaluating Redwood for patient-facing summarization routes so latency and compliance are big.
[00:20] Liam (AtlasHealth): Liam, platform eng, we'll own network / VPC and data egress.
[00:24] Nina (AtlasHealth): Nina, security and compliance.
[00:27] Jordan: awesome, and from our side Priya and Marco will go deep on spans and dashboards.
[00:32] Priya (Redwood SE): hi! I'll start with the high-level design then we can jump into examples and the pros/cons.

[00:40] Priya: so we instrument the inference pipeline with OpenTelemetry - at a minimum we emit a span per request, and optionally we can emit spans per token emission if you want token-level timing and KV cache hit visibility. token spans are higher cardinality but give you per-token latency, batching effects, and whether the kv cache short-circuited generation.
[01:05] Ethan (AtlasHealth): quick q — by token-level do you mean literally each token gets its own span? isn't that going to explode traces?
[01:12] Priya: yes it can; we recommend two patterns: 1) full token-level spans for short pilot workloads (low QPS) or targeted prompt sets, 2) sampled token spans — e.g., 1 in N requests or adaptive sampling triggered on anomalies. you can also emit token metrics aggregated server-side (counts, histograms) instead of full spans.
[01:35] Marco (Redwood SRE): to add — we often attach attributes at both request-span and token-span level: model variant, seq_len, batch_size, kv_cache_hit=true/false, quantization (int8/float16), gpu_type. that lets dashboards pivot on these dimensions.
[01:50] Nina: what's the overhead here? CPU and network for OTLP?
[01:54] Marco: good question. token spans are more bytes and items — in our tests full token spans increased egress by ~3–6x depending on token rate. CPU overhead depends on exporter (we recommend OTLP exporter to a local collector sidecar to buffer and batch). for high-throughput we prefer metrics + sparse spans: metrics for p50/p95/p99 token latency and a small number of sampled spans for traces.
[02:18] Liam: about the collector — inside our VPC we need to keep things private. can we run the collector inside VPC and push to our managed observability?
[02:25] Jordan: yes, we support sidecar or daemonset collectors inside your VPC/on-prem. Redwood can send OTLP to your collector over TLS; we also support mTLS if you want mutual TLS between runtime and collector. for private deployments we can also integrate with on-prem Tempo/Jaeger/Grafana stacks and avoid any public egress.
[02:45] Samira: how do you correlate tokens to business-level IDs? we need to tie generations to patient IDs but obviously not send PHI in plain text.
[02:52] Priya: we recommend generating an internal correlation id per request and attaching it as a span attribute. do not send PHI as attributes; instead send a hashed identifier or a pointer that your systems can map internally. we also support PII filters in the collector to redact attributes.
[03:10] Ethan: does Redwood expose token-level metrics like tokens/sec, kv cache hit-rate, avg token latency as Prometheus metrics?
[03:17] Marco: yes, we export aggregated metrics in Prometheus format (or OTLP metrics). common metrics: redwood_generation_tokens_total, redwood_generation_token_latency_seconds_bucket (histogram), redwood_kv_cache_hits_total, redwood_batch_size_distribution. those map well into Grafana dashboards.
[03:36] Priya: and for model-level insights we emit per-model and per-variant labels — note cardinality concerns: having labels for prompt_id or user_id can blow up cardinality so we avoid high-cardinality labels in metrics. use spans for high-cardinality but sampled traces.
[03:55] Samira: can you show an example span structure?
[03:59] Priya: sure — high-level: span name = "redwood.generation.request" with attributes: request_id, model_name, model_variant, seq_len, input_token_count, batch_size. nested token spans "redwood.generation.token" attributes: token_index, kv_cache_hit, token_generation_ms, sampler_temperature. we'll paste exact examples in the sample repo.
[04:28] [screen share pause — Jordan shares slide deck link: https://redwood.app/decks/observability-overview ]
[04:40] Jordan: slide 6 shows an example Grafana dashboard built from these metrics — top row p50/p95/p99 latency, second row tokens/sec, kv cache hit-rate, bottom row quantization effects (latency delta) and batch size heatmap.
[04:55] Liam: speaking of quantization — how visible is the impact of int8 vs fp16 on latency and quality in your traces?
[05:02] Marco: we emit an attribute quantization_profile on request spans and we correlate with token latency histograms and quality regressions (from our eval hooks). quantization usually reduces latency, but you can see micro-regressions in output quality; we tie that to eval sets and generate regression alerts.
[05:20] Priya: also note we record kernel selection metadata — e.g., kernel_vendor: cuFFT-like, attention_impl: flash_attention_v2 — so you can see when a particular kernel causes latency spikes on certain sequences.
[05:35] Samira: we want dashboards in our Grafana with alerting; can you ship dashboard JSON?
[05:39] Marco: yes, I'll export the Grafana dashboard JSON and share. it includes alert rules for p95 latency > X ms, kv cache hit-rate < Y%, and token tail latency anomalies.
[05:52] Nina: audit logs and retention — how long do these traces/metrics live and can we set retention per-namespace for compliance?
[05:59] Jordan: retention is configurable. for hosted we offer default retention windows; for private deployments you control retention. we can also set redact/PII stripping at ingestion. for SOC2 concerns we keep access logs and can forward audit logs to your SIEM.
[06:13] Ethan: any recommendations for sampling config? we're expecting bursts up to 2000 QPS on some endpoints.
[06:20] Priya: at 2k QPS you almost certainly want aggregated metrics + light sampling. recommendation: metrics always on, request-level spans sampled at 5-10% for normal ops, token-level spans sampled at 0.1-1% or only when latency > threshold. adaptive sampling is useful — increase sampling when p95 spikes.
[06:38] Marco: plus use a local collector with a write-behind buffer and backpressure; we have configs to drop token spans under overload to preserve request throughput.
[06:47] Liam: curious about batching visibility — can I see per-batch size distribution and how it impacts token latency?
[06:53] Priya: yes, we emit batch_size as a label and a distribution metric; the dashboard heatmap shows latency vs batch size. you can correlate with queue_time_ms to see if batching is adding queueing delay.
[07:08] Samira: we use dedicated GPU pools for latency-sensitive routes; how do rollouts and model variants show up?
[07:13] Marco: per-variant labels make it straightforward to compare p95 across variants in Grafana. rollouts create new model_variant tags and you can run canary rules — the console will also mark rollout percent which we can export as metric.
[07:25] [08:00] Interruption / crosstalk as Samira asks about a PoC timeline and Jordan confirms pilot logistics.

[08:20] Priya: practical demo — here's a live trace we captured: traced one request with token spans turned on. you can see token 0 took 12ms, tokens 1–4 8–10ms each, token 5 had a kv cache hit and was 2ms. note how token spans let you pinpoint where the kv cache saved work.
[08:48] Ethan: awesome — is kv cache hit a boolean attr or more detailed?
[08:52] Priya: boolean plus cache_lookup_time_ms and cache_key_size bytes. we also optionally log cache miss reasons (evicted, not found, prefix mismatch).
[09:05] Jordan: one pitfall we see — people put prompt_id as a metric label; that creates cardinality explosions. prefer storing prompt_id in spans or in a low-volume tag that you forward to your internal mapping service.
[09:18] Nina: for on-prem installs, what's the recommendation to avoid egress?
[09:22] Marco: deploy the collector as a daemonset inside the cluster and point Redwood runtime to the local OTLP endpoint. for air-gapped, we provide an on-prem bundle with a local metrics backend and the console in a private network. no public egress required.
[09:36] Ethan: what about span latency — will tracing add latency to generation?
[09:40] Priya: tracing itself is async — we don't block generation on exporting spans. overhead is mostly CPU for span creation and memory. the main risk is exporter saturation causing backpressure; that's why we recommend local buffering and non-blocking exporters.
[09:55] Liam: can you demo an alert scenario — say p95 spike due to kernel regression?
[10:00] Marco: sure — here's an example alert flow: p95 > threshold triggers an alert; we open a Grafana panel showing recent traces sampled. from those traces we see kernel selection attr changed to new_attention_impl; we correlate with deployments and roll back. we can wire alerts into PagerDuty and include a link to the sampled trace.
[10:20] Priya: also we tag spans with runtime version and kernel metadata so rollbacks are traceable.

[10:35] Samira: security — are spans encrypted at rest and in transit?
[10:38] Marco: OTLP over TLS encrypts in transit. for at-rest encryption that's your observability backend config (Grafana/Tempo). for hosted we support server-side encryption and KMS-managed keys. we can also PII-redact in the collector before persistence.
[10:55] Nina: who has access controls for traces in Redwood console?
[10:58] Jordan: RBAC in the console maps to your SSO; for private deployments you can integrate with SAML/SCIM and map teams to roles. traces and metrics access can be restricted by team/namespace.

[11:15] Ethan: one more question — do you surface quantization-induced quality regressions automatically?
11:21 Priya: yes we run evals continuously against configured prompt sets and if quality metrics degrade beyond threshold we trigger a quality regression alert and annotate affected traces and model variants.

[11:35] Jordan: ok time for recap and next steps.
[11:38] Jordan: recap — we'll provide sample instrumentation repo (OpenTelemetry spans + Prometheus metrics), Grafana dashboard JSON, and security docs on collector deployment and mTLS. AtlasHealth to provide prompt sets and QPS profiles; Redwood to run 1-week pilot with token sampling enabled and share metrics.
[11:55] Samira: sounds good we'll get prompt sets to Ethan and he'll send to Priya.
[11:59] Jordan: I'll schedule follow-up for next Wednesday to review pilot results and security review. expect docs from us by Friday.
[12:06] meeting end

Notes / imperfections: transcription includes occasional mis-typed words (e.g., "k v cache", "cahe") and a few fused sentences; speaker labels are accurate but short forms used. Links shared: deck and sample repo references (will be sent in follow-up).
